column3: At Ásfjord the creditors' agent decides which wrongs are worth pursuing, and the debts come first.
This account of Ásfjord's safety comes from a first survey, so trouble the hamlet keeps from newcomers may be missing from it.
Ásfjord keeps armed people on an open frontier, which means the defense is reactive: whatever comes chooses where the fighting happens, and the hamlet arrives afterwards.
The armed townspeople you meet at Ásfjord are capable on their own ground and have never stood in a line with anyone.
If you are wronged at Ásfjord, there is nowhere to take it, and no local is surprised.
The hamlet could not pay for a bad month at Ásfjord, and the people who would have to be paid know it.
Ásfjord is unfortified. There is no perimeter, which means the hamlet cannot control entry and cannot make a chokepoint of anything.
Ásfjord's people take up arms when they must and go back to work after; they are not soldiers by trade.
Ásfjord retains no specialists. Whatever comes out of the country is met by whoever the hamlet has, whether or not they are the right answer to it.
Ásfjord keeps no defence against anything it cannot see.
Ásfjord has not been attacked lately, and if it were, it would struggle to hold.
Ásfjord pays its creditors first and its defence with what is left, and what is left shrinks each year.
Life in the hamlet goes on through the crisis: people work, eat and sleep, and the defence makes do with what is left over.
Ásfjord is too small to wall and knows it; the hamlet's safety is its neighbours, its distance, and its unimportance.
Ásfjord's books record no gang, guild or racket: what wrongdoing the hamlet has, people do on their own account.
No criminal's money appears in the Free Elder Council's accounts at Ásfjord, so what the hall spends is spent on the hamlet.
